findings.text: Decision 4 resolves `nodes.n.output.p...` (and `hook.output.*`) to `fields[p]` when `p` is an own key, and to `output` otherwise. It never says what a reference to the whole output with an empty path (`nodes.n.output`, `hook.output`) carries. The taken `Ref` type allows `path: []` for `root: "node"`, and the shown part of the format spec neither forbids nor tests `nodes.a.output` with no path. Followed as written, `${{ nodes.fetch_invoice.output }}` would carry `[]`, because RF-1's `fetch_invoice` has `output` `[]` while its `raw_text` and `vendor_name` fields are `untrusted`. That would let data pass through as trusted in a fail-closed security algebra. The spec needs a rule for this case (for example, join `output` with every `fields` entry), plus a scenario that tests it.

Decision 6 requires both functions to be total for any plain-JSON document and to fail closed. But no rule covers malformed hook structures: `flow.hooks` that is not an array (Decision 7 takes `flow.hooks.length`, so a string would count characters), a rule that is not an object, a `match` that is missing or not an object, a selector field that is not a list, a node `pre`/`post` that is not an array, a hook entry that is not an object, or a hook `kind` that is neither `code` nor `block`. These choices change taint (does a malformed rule match every node? Does an unknown hook kind count as a code hook that widens output?) and they change capability sites. No scenario covers any of them, so an implementer could pick a fail-open reading and every test would still pass.

design.md § Interfaces says `from` is "the producing node (for `nodes.*` and `hook.output.*`)". The scenario "Unknown and malformed input fails closed" expects `from: null` for `nodes.ghost.output.x`. The rule should say that a missing node gives `from: null`.

Decision 7 checks the limits "before any work", but the edge count includes "every applying hook, once per wrapped node". Deciding which hooks apply under `effect` selectors needs catalogue lookups, so catalogue calls (and catalogue exceptions) can happen before the edge-limit check. The order of catalogue calls against the limit checks is not fixed.

findings.text: Scenario "Canonical JSON keeps real differences and unusual keys" changes "the order of `outcomes`" and "a `routes` entry of a code hook". The canonical sample it starts from (a `fetch` block, an `extract` node, a node-level `post` block hook, and a flow-level `pre` code hook with only `input` and `source`) has no `llm.decide` node with `outcomes` and no `routes`. The test plan's standard sample (a block, an `llm.extract`, a `switch`, an `end`) has neither. The implementer has to extend the sample, and the spec does not say how.

In scenario "Value fields and successors per node kind", the expected `successorFields` result for the `switch` (`/cases/k` then `/default`) gives no `producesOutput` value, while every other case gives one. The successor tables for `code`, `llm.*`, `agent`, `foreach`, `subflow`, `delegate` and `wait` are only described as "the seed's `graph.ts` pair". That works only because the seed is readable.

Decision 2 says every value other than plain objects, arrays, strings, finite numbers, booleans and null is `FORMAT_NOT_JSON`, and it singles out only an array element `undefined`. Decision 5 and the scenario expect `canonicalJson({ a: undefined, b: 1 })` to return `{"b":1}`. So `findJsonProblem` must accept an `undefined` object property, but Decision 2 does not say so.

`requiredSuccessorFields("delegate")` returns `["next", "on_timeout"]`, while `DelegateNode` types `on_timeout` as optional. In contrast, `HumanFormNode` types `on_timeout` as required. The meaning of "required" next to the permissive types is not stated.

Decision 1 puts only `doc.toJS` inside try/catch, and its throw mapping (`ReferenceError` to ALIAS_LIMIT, `RangeError` to TOO_DEEP) is stated for `toJS` only. For YAML nested 100,000 deep, `parseDocument` itself may overflow the stack. The scenario expects `FORMAT_TOO_DEEP`, so the same try/catch and mapping must cover `parseDocument`. Decision 1 also says `findJsonProblem(doc, ...)` walks `doc` (the YAML Document) where it means the JS value, and its JSON branch does not mention the walk that Decision 2 requires.

`canonicalizeFlow` normalises references through `valueFields`/`hookValueFields` on `nodes` and `hooks`. The spec does not say what happens when `nodes` or `hooks` is missing or is not an object or array (for example `{ a: 1 }` in the hash scenario). Skipping normalisation is the only reading that fits the golden hash, but it is not stated. It is also not stated whether references nested deeper inside a value field (for example `with.a.b`) are normalised.

Decision 10 does not list "the hook fields" or "the reference roots and scopes" term by term. It is unclear, for example, whether the node root appears as `nodes` (the syntax) or `node` (the `Ref.root` value), and which `HookSelector`/`HookWhen`/`HookDef` fields are included. The order of `documentedTerms()` is therefore underdetermined. This does not matter much because the doc and its test are written together.
The `FormatError.name` value is not fixed. `canonicalEqual` behaviour on a non-JSON input (does it throw `FormatError` or return false?) is not stated.

The scenario expects `YAML a: &x [*x]` to give `FORMAT_TOO_DEEP`, which depends on `yaml` 2.9.1 producing a cyclic value rather than tripping its alias count (`ReferenceError`, which would give `FORMAT_ALIAS_LIMIT`). Design states it was checked against 2.9.1; this cannot be confirmed from the material.

findings.text: Scenario "Canonical JSON keeps real differences and unusual keys" changes "the order of `outcomes`" and "a `routes` entry of a code hook". The test plan's standard sample (a block, an `llm.extract`, a `switch`, an `end`) has neither. The implementer has to extend the sample, and the spec does not say how.

In scenario "Value fields and successors per node kind", the expected `successorFields` result for the `switch` (`/cases/k` then `/default`) gives no `producesOutput` value, while every other case gives one. The successor tables for `code`, `llm.*`, `agent`, `foreach`, `subflow`, `delegate` and `wait` are only described as "the seed's `graph.ts` pair". That works only because the seed is readable.

Decision 2 says every value other than plain objects, arrays, strings, finite numbers, booleans and null is `FORMAT_NOT_JSON`, and it singles out only an array element `undefined`. Decision 5 and the scenario expect `canonicalJson({ a: undefined, b: 1 })` to return `{"b":1}`. So `findJsonProblem` must accept an `undefined` object property, but Decision 2 does not say so.

`requiredSuccessorFields("delegate")` returns `["next", "on_timeout"]`, while `DelegateNode` types `on_timeout` as optional. In contrast, `HumanFormNode` types `on_timeout` as required. The meaning of "required" next to the permissive types is not stated.

Decision 1 puts only `doc.toJS` inside try/catch, and its throw mapping (`ReferenceError` to ALIAS_LIMIT, `RangeError` to TOO_DEEP) is stated for `toJS` only. For YAML nested 100,000 deep, `parseDocument` itself may overflow the stack. The scenario expects `FORMAT_TOO_DEEP`, so the same try/catch and mapping must cover `parseDocument`. Decision 1 also says `findJsonProblem(doc, ...)` walks `doc` (the YAML Document) where it means the JS value, and its JSON branch does not mention the walk that Decision 2 requires.

`canonicalizeFlow` normalises references through `valueFields`/`hookValueFields` on `nodes` and `hooks`. The spec does not say what happens when `nodes` or `hooks` is missing or is not an object or array (for example `{ a: 1 }` in the hash scenario). Skipping normalisation is the only reading that fits the golden hash, but it is not stated. It is also not stated whether references nested deeper inside a value field (for example `with.a.b`) are normalised.

Decision 10 does not list "the hook fields" or "the reference roots and scopes" term by term. It is unclear, for example, whether the node root appears as `nodes` (the syntax) or `node` (the `Ref.root` value), and which `HookSelector`/`HookWhen`/`HookDef` fields are included. The order of `documentedTerms()` is therefore underdetermined. This does not matter much because the doc and its test are written together.
The `FormatError.name` value is not fixed. `canonicalEqual` behaviour on a non-JSON input (does it throw `FormatError` or return false?) is not stated.

The scenario expects `YAML a: &x [*x]` to give `FORMAT_TOO_DEEP`, which depends on `yaml` 2.9.1 producing a cyclic value rather than tripping its alias count (`ReferenceError`, which would give `FORMAT_ALIAS_LIMIT`). findings.text: Scenario "Canonical JSON keeps real differences and unusual keys" changes "the order of `outcomes`" and "a `routes` entry of a code hook". The canonical sample it starts from (a `fetch` block, an `extract` node, a node-level `post` block hook, and a flow-level `pre` code hook with only `input` and `source`) has no `llm.decide` node with `outcomes` and no `routes`. The test plan's standard sample (a block, an `llm.extract`, a `switch`, an `end`) has neither. The implementer has to extend the sample, and the spec does not say how.

In scenario "Value fields and successors per node kind", the expected `successorFields` result for the `switch` (`/cases/k` then `/default`) gives no `producesOutput` value, while every other case gives one. The successor tables for `code`, `llm.*`, `agent`, `foreach`, `subflow`, `delegate` and `wait` are only described as "the seed's `graph.ts` pair". That works only because the seed is readable.

Decision 2 says every value other than plain objects, arrays, strings, finite numbers, booleans and null is `FORMAT_NOT_JSON`, and it singles out only an array element `undefined`. Decision 5 and the scenario expect `canonicalJson({ a: undefined, b: 1 })` to return `{"b":1}`. So `findJsonProblem` must accept an `undefined` object property, but Decision 2 does not say so.

`requiredSuccessorFields("delegate")` returns `["next", "on_timeout"]`, while `DelegateNode` types `on_timeout` as optional. In contrast, `HumanFormNode` types `on_timeout` as required. The meaning of "required" next to the permissive types is not stated.

Decision 1 puts only `doc.toJS` inside try/catch, and its throw mapping (`ReferenceError` to ALIAS_LIMIT, `RangeError` to TOO_DEEP) is stated for `toJS` only. For YAML nested 100,000 deep, `parseDocument` itself may overflow the stack. The scenario expects `FORMAT_TOO_DEEP`, so the same try/catch and mapping must cover `parseDocument`. Decision 1 also says `findJsonProblem(doc, ...)` walks `doc` (the YAML Document) where it means the JS value, and its JSON branch does not mention the walk that Decision 2 requires.

`canonicalizeFlow` normalises references through `valueFields`/`hookValueFields` on `nodes` and `hooks`. The spec does not say what happens when `nodes` or `hooks` is missing or is not an object or array (for example `{ a: 1 }` in the hash scenario). Skipping normalisation is the only reading that fits the golden hash, but it is not stated. It is also not stated whether references nested deeper inside a value field (for example `with.a.b`) are normalised.

Decision 10 does not list "the hook fields" or "the reference roots and scopes" term by term. It is unclear, for example, whether the node root appears as `nodes` (the syntax) or `node` (the `Ref.root` value), and which `HookSelector`/`HookWhen`/`HookDef` fields are included. The order of `documentedTerms()` is therefore underdetermined. This does not matter much because the doc and its test are written together.
The `FormatError.name` value is not fixed. `canonicalEqual` behaviour on a non-JSON input (does it throw `FormatError` or return false?) is not stated.

The scenario expects `YAML a: &x [*x]` to give `FORMAT_TOO_DEEP`, which depends on `yaml` 2.9.1 producing a cyclic value rather than tripping its alias count (`ReferenceError`, which would give `FORMAT_ALIAS_LIMIT`). Design states it was checked against 2.9.1; this cannot be confirmed from the material.

findings.text: In the scenario "Validation failures change nothing", catalogueFor rejects, and then validating an unknown hash, or version 1's hash under flow `other`, must give 404. If catalogueFor still rejects during those later calls, loading the catalogue first gives 500 instead of 404. The scenario's result is clear, so an implementer can meet it by checking existence first, but the spec should state the order: resource loader, then version lookup, then catalogueFor, then validateVersion.

Most of the parse-refusal details carry `message` (and `line`/`column`).
